# Tile Runner: movement, collision and pickups (c)

Implement can_enter and runner_step. w/a/s/d move one cell; walls and out-of-bounds destinations block movement. Collect each C only once (coins is a two-bit mask: (3,4)=bit 0, (5,4)=bit 1). Reaching G at (7,1) wins only after both pickups. Each input increments ticks and records whether movement succeeded; an already-won game remains unchanged. The terminal executable calls your functions for every action. First make the collision test fail visibly, then repair the mechanics, play a winning route and export its native frames.

Edit `mechanics.c`. `model.h` defines the fixed-size state; it owns its arrays, and callbacks borrow a mutable pointer/reference to it. No heap-owned gameplay buffers are returned. The main program calls your mechanics for every input; it does not implement a second version of the game.

Build: `cc -std=c17 mechanics.c main.c -o game`
Play: `./game` (press Enter after each action; q exits).
Tests: `cc -std=c17 mechanics.c tests.c -o project-tests && ./project-tests`
Replay: `./game --replay sssddddddwww > replay.ndjson`

Replay files contain a header followed by native-computed JSON frames. Import replay.ndjson on the project page; its viewer displays those frames without simulating movement, cooldowns or enemies.

Requirements: a C17 compiler. Windows: executable names may end in .exe; use game.exe/project-tests.exe instead of ./game/./project-tests.

The starter compiles and deliberately fails named tests. Implement the mechanics, run tests, then play and export your own replay. The reference and explanation stay on the website; the starter download does not replace your work with the solution.

explanation: can_enter validates bounds before indexing the borrowed immutable board. runner_step maps one action to a cardinal offset, records the tick, and commits position only when can_enter allows the destination. Pickup bits make repeated visits idempotent. The exit check uses the resulting native state; entering G without both bits cannot win. main calls this callback for both interactive input and replay export, so changing collision/pickup code changes the game and exported frames.
